item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Ozon next in Kyiv’s sights as sheds of Wildberries rival burn
item.description:
Putin decree lets Russian state scoop up companies that come under attack; ‘dig into our stocks’ of Patriots, British PM urges allies. What we know on day 1,644

Ukraine has targeted four more warehouses of Ozon – Russia’s second-largest online retailer after Wildberries, which has itself been crippled by Ukrainian attacks. Ozon’s shares fell by almost 30% on Monday ​after it reported strikes in southern Russia that brought to six the number of its facilities targeted within three days. Ozon said a logistics hub in Makhachkala in Dagestan was on fire and had halted operations after a drone attack in which “several people” were injured. Another was on fire in Enem on the outskirts of the city of Krasnodar, while workers were evacuated from warehouses that came under attack in ​Adygeysk, in the Adygeya region, and in Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.

In earlier events, drone strikes halted work at an Ozon ‌logistics centre in the Samara region and another ‌in the Orenburg region. Financial analysts said that unlike privately owned Wildberries, which has the backing of ​state-owned bank VTB, Ozon’s main shareholder AFK Sistema has a large debt and is unlikely to provide substantial support. Before the latest Ozon attacks, Vladimir Putin promised state help in the restoration of warehouses “at a new technological level” and asked the government to design a programme to help the sector. The EU imposed sanctions on Ozon’s and Wildberries’ financial units on 24 July.

Putin has geared up the Russian state to seize control of companies like Wildberries and Ozon, as well as fuel companies and transport operators, by deeming them too poorly protected from Ukrainian attacks. Special powers set out in a presidential decree will allow ⁠the state to take charge of them at a time when Ukraine has stepped up drone ⁠attacks on oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses. The state will be able to seize physical and financial assets, ‌and assume formal ownership ‌rights, if entities responsible for such facilities are judged to have failed to protect them and are too slow to repair them after any attack. It applies to fuel, energy, industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities and other objects regarded as critically important for security and economic stability.

The ⁠Ukrainian military struck ⁠a ⁠Russian Mig-29 fighter ​plane and two ⁠Russian vessels in the Black ⁠Sea, ​Ukraine’s ‌drone ‌forces commander ‌Robert Brovdi said on Monday. It is the third Russian warplane hit in two days. Brovdi said on the ‌Telegram app that one ​of the vessels attacked was ⁠a tanker ​and the ​other ​was a ​bulk ‌carrier. Ukraine’s ⁠military struck a ⁠Russian military ⁠plant ​at Kamensky in the Rostov ⁠region, causing ⁠a ​fire, the ‌Ukrainian ‌general staff ‌said. The plant ​produces solid rocket ​fuel for Russian weapons.

The Perm oil refinery, Russia’s seventh-largest by volume, has shut down after a Ukrainian drone attack on 21 August, two industry sources ⁠told Reuters. The primary CDU-4 unit, which accounts for almost 40% of the plant’s capacity, stopped working on that day. Repair ‌works could take between one and two weeks. Another primary refining unit, CDU-5, which accounts for 34% of ​the plant’s capacity, has been idle since a 29 July drone attack. Lukoil, which controls the refinery, ​did not ​reply to a request for ​comment. The plant usually makes millions of tonnes of petrol and diesel.

Andy Burnham urged Ukraine’s allies to “dig into our own stocks” to provide it with more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying it “needs more help to protect its people right now”. The British prime minister chaired his first meeting of the “coalition of the willing” in Kyiv as Ukraine celebrated its independence day. Burnham said the coalition was “doing everything we can all do and working with our allies outside of this coalition to dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”. He called on the US Congress to “ratchet up” economic pressure on Russia as it struggles with a record budget deficit and declining oil revenues.

Ten Ukrainian prisoners of war who were thought to be missing in action have been released in a prisoner exchange, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He did not mention Russia in his statement, saying only that the prisoners had been released via Belarus, one of Moscow’s closest allies. Russia did not immediately say if Kyiv had returned soldiers in the exchange.

item.title: Israel making Lebanon a burned out hellscape and US paying for it
item.description:
For two years, Israel's war in Lebanon has been measured largely in a human toll: the dead, the wounded, the displaced. What has drawn far less attention is the destruction of the land itself.

Across southern Lebanon, a combination of incendiary munitions, systematic demolitions, and now aerial herbicide spraying has degraded large stretches of Lebanese territory to the point where it is difficult to farm, unsafe to inhabit, and in many places, unrecognizable.

American money and American weapons are behind nearly all of it.

Since the attacks on Lebanon escalated in late 2024, Israeli forces have made extensive use of white phosphorus munitions across the south of Lebanon. The Israeli military's stated rationale is that phosphorus shells serve as smoke screens to mask troop movements and deny Hezbollah fighters cover; officials have denied using them intentionally to start fires.

But that rationale does not hold up well against the pattern of use. Investigations by outlets including Al Jazeera have documented phosphorus shelling that torched oak and pine forests, destroyed decades- and centuries-old olive groves, and left soil contaminated with lead and other heavy metals. These effects persist long after any potential tactical need for concealment has passed.

Lebanon's National Council for Scientific Research has estimated $25 billion in environmental damages from strikes between 2023 and 2024 alone, including thousands of hectares of destroyed forest and orchard. Reporting from the border village of Ayta ash-Shaab documented the destruction of the Monk Forest, one of the last intact woodland refuges in the border zone, through phosphorus shelling and bulldozing that left what satellite imagery shows as white craters scattered across what had been continuous forest cover.

Where munitions have not flattened border villages outright, Israeli forces have often finished the job with remote-detonated explosives that level entire neighborhoods in seconds. Israel's official justification is narrower than the phosphorus rationale: that Hezbollah has embedded military infrastructure – tunnels, weapons caches, command posts – inside civilian buildings over decades. But the scale, method, and permanence of what has followed makes that justification fall flat.

The Guardian reviewed footage of mass detonations in the villages of Taybeh, Naqoura, and Deir Seryan, in each case razing entire villages to the ground in a single blast rather than targeting individual structures; further mass detonations have been filmed and published by the Israeli military itself in Mhaibib and Majdal Zoun, in one case showing soldiers celebrating a village's destruction on camera.

In Adaisseh and Kfar Kila, Lebanese state media reported explosions large enough that a single underground detonation was strong enough to trigger earthquake-warning systems in Israel.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz has stated plainly that all homes in Lebanese border villages will be destroyed, comparing the plan to the demolition of Rafah and Beit Hanoun in Gaza, where the Israeli military leveled roughly 90% of homes. Journalist Lylla Younes, reporting from her own family's region near Bint Jbeil, described entire villages reduced to “moonscapes,” terrain so thoroughly cratered and flattened that residents have resorted to purchasing satellite imagery just to determine whether their homes still exist, since they cannot physically reach the villages to check.

The detonations are also setting the land on fire, independent of the phosphorus shelling described above. “What our documentation increasingly shows, particularly over the past two months, is a sharp rise in fires coinciding with or following large-scale Israeli detonations and the demolition of entire neighbourhoods, particularly in occupied border areas and their immediate surroundings,” said Dr. Hisham Younes, president of Green Southerners, a Lebanese environmental organization working to protect South Lebanon's natural heritage. “But the destruction is not confined to these areas; it extends further into different parts of South Lebanon.”

Israeli military maps released this spring marked a red line running through 21 villages and barred residents from returning to more than 50 others. A CNN review of satellite imagery identified newly built Israeli forward operating bases positioned inside Lebanese territory. NPR's reporting from the village of Mansouri described a town center reduced to rubble – shops blown open, homes crumpled, a mosque burned with its minaret split in two – six miles from the border but now sitting inside the militarized "yellow line."

U.N. human rights experts have described the pattern of blanket evacuation orders and systematic housing destruction as consistent with what has happened in Gaza, and rights groups have said the mass remote detonations, as distinct from targeted demolitions, could amount to wanton destruction under the laws of war.

In early 2026, Israel added a third tactic: aerial spraying of glyphosate, a controversial herbicide, across roughly 11 miles of the southern border. Israeli officials described this to Lebanon’s U.N. peacekeeping mission as routine vegetation management using “approved substances,” intended to clear dense brush that could conceal infiltration. Lebanon's agriculture ministry found levels 20 to 50 times higher than normal agricultural use, which could sterilize soil and prevent regrowth for years. Independent Dutch research organization PAX estimated between 1,000 and 1,600 acres of land affected on the Syrian side of the border alone, with additional spraying on the Lebanese side that satellite imagery did not fully capture.

Israel initially told U.N. peacekeepers the sprayed substance was “non-toxic.” Laboratory testing subsequently confirmed Israel’s use of glyphosate, a chemical the World Health Organization's cancer research arm classifies as probably carcinogenic to humans, which helps explain why it is banned outright in both Lebanon and the European Union.

The herbicide is blanketing land already stressed by years of phosphorus and heavy-metal contamination, compounding damage to soil, pollinators, and an agricultural economy that roughly 80% of southern Lebanon depends on. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun called the spraying “a flagrant violation of Lebanese sovereignty and an environmental and health crime.”

Each of these three tactics has an official Israeli justification that sounds reasonable in isolation: smoke screens, tunnel denial, brush clearing. What is harder to explain is why, in each case, the actual scale and persistence of the harm so far exceeds what the stated rationale requires.

“Heavy bombardment, incendiary attacks including white phosphorus, demolitions and chemical spraying have destroyed, contaminated and degraded these landscapes, while the extensive use of explosives has physically reshaped the terrain itself,” Younes said. “Taken together, we see this as a systematic process of destruction and place erasure, progressively dismantling the ecological and physical foundations that make return, recovery and continued life possible”

The practical result is a southern Lebanon that an estimated 600,000 residents, per Israel's own defense minister, will not be permitted to return to, in villages that in some cases no longer exist in a form their own residents can identify from satellite imagery.

This is not the conduct of a few rogue units. It is what the entire U.S.-armed Israeli military has done, systematically, for two years, and it calls for a systemic response.

Most of what's being destroyed won't recover in any of our lifetimes, if it recovers at all. The response has to match the scale of the destruction: cut off the military aid sustaining it, before it's too late.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy orders military to triple daily long-range strikes on Russia
item.description:
Kyiv to ramp up attacks; Russian gasoline production drops after drone strikes; Fedorov joins Italy’s defence ministry. What we know on day 1,648

⁠Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ⁠​he has ⁠ordered his military to increase its ⁠long-range ​drone ‌strikes ‌against Russia to ‌1,000 per day, up from about 300 currently. “There ‌needs to be more: ​there is a concrete goal, ⁠and we will fulfil ​this ​task,” the Ukrainian president ​declared ​on Friday in ‌his ​evening address.

Russia’s ⁠gasoline production fell ​to about 70% of domestic consumption levels by the end of August after a series of drone attacks forced major refineries to suspend operations, according to two ⁠industry sources who spoke to Reuters. After a brief respite at the end of July, when some local authorities ​began easing or lifting restrictions on fuel sales, shortages ‌returned to Russian regions in ‌August. Over the past week, drones ‌struck and halted operations at several major refineries, including plants in Perm, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl, all significant producers of motor gasoline.

Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said. While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the past two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured, Peter Walker writes.

Recent Russian air attacks have destroyed about 90% of retailers’ food logistics in Ukraine, ⁠Kyiv’s agricultural minister said on Friday. Both countries have stepped up strikes in recent weeks on economic targets such as major retailers, with Russia targeting warehouses for ⁠Ukraine’s premier supermarket chains, ⁠top postal service and home-goods ​stores. “As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn’t mean Ukrainians will be left without food,” farm minister Taras Vysotskyi was cited by ⁠the Ukrinform agency as saying. His comments to reporters in Kyiv are the most frank official assessment of the damage Russia’s escalating strikes have brought on Ukraine’s increasingly fragile economy in the fifth year of war.

Ukraine has stored ⁠14.6bn cubic metres ​of gas ⁠in underground storage, enough ⁠for ​the upcoming ‌winter ‌season, the ‌country’s energy minister said. “Ukraine has stockpiled ‌natural gas for ​the baseline scenario for getting ⁠through the ​winter,” Denys ​Shmyhal ​said ​on Friday.

Authorities ⁠in Russia’s Rostov region ⁠declared a ⁠state ​of emergency on Friday, ⁠saying port closures and disruptions ⁠to navigation ​in ‌the ‌Azov-Black Sea basin had ‌led to a significant accumulation of agricultural products at farms. The ‌regional government said on ​Telegram an emergency response had been introduced ⁠across the ​region, without ​going into ​more detail.

Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has ⁠accepted a role as innovation adviser at Italy’s Defence Ministry, officials said ⁠on ​Friday. Italy’s defence minister Guido Crosetto had disclosed the offer shortly after Fedorov ⁠was dismissed in July. Fedorov, 35, was fired six months after his appointment, having ​initiated reforms around procurement and mobilisation that put him on a collision course with the military establishment and political rivals.

The UN nuclear ⁠watchdog said on Friday it had ⁠been informed ⁠of ​three drone incidents at Russian-held Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power plant in south-eastern Ukraine ⁠earlier this week. The International ​Atomic ‌Energy Agency said a drone attack ‌on 25 August reportedly occurred near the plant’s cooling pond, injuring two plant employees, ‌while two other drones on 26 August ​reportedly struck the site’s dry spent nuclear fuel storage area ⁠and the sprinkling ​device of ​the power ​units system. Radiation levels at ​the ‌Zaporizhzhia ​plant ​remained normal, the watchdog added.

Russian forces on Friday resumed their drone barrage of Ukraine’s Kyiv region, hitting more than a dozen apartment buildings and storage depots in a second straight day of aerial attacks, officials said. Russian strikes in the Kyiv region damaged 14 warehouses, 16 private houses, three apartment buildings and 16 vehicles, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv regional military administration, said Friday.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Nuclear plant has lost power and running on generators, UN watchdog says
item.description:
Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia plant has 10-day diesel supply on site; Kyiv investigates deadly attack on warehouse. What we know on day 1,649

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week and is now relying on emergency diesel generators, the UN’s nuclear watchdog says. The plant, which needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool, has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday.

“The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” said agency director general Rafael Grossi. “The current situation once again shows why reliable external power and secure supply routes are indispensable for nuclear safety and security.” The plant had been supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA added.

Zaporizhzhia lost its regular power supply “following military activity on the northern side of the Dnipro River”, the statement said. The IAEA said it was trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines. The plant, in southern Ukraine, was seized by the Russian army in March 2022 and its six reactors have been shut down since that year.

Germany is reportedly preparing to blame Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport and impose sanctions on Russian entities. Friedrich Merz’s government is expected to announce the “extensive” measures in the next week, Politico reports, potentially alongside a new EU sanctions package.

Ukrainian prosecutors have opened an investigation into why munitions were stored so close to homes after a deadly Russian attack on a warehouse storing “explosive objects” near Kyiv’s western suburbs. At least 37 people were killed in the attack on the warehouse in Myla on Friday, making it the war’s deadliest attack this year, Donna Ferguson reports.

The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings, including a care home for elderly and disabled people, and sparked a huge fire and explosions in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region. The regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said a further 42 people, including four children, had been injured in the strike.

The warehouse was a depot owned by the Ukrainian military and stored shells, drones and other munitions, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a video address. “The first impact was on a place where ammunition was being stored that absolutely should not have been there – a depot of the defence forces. [There was] detonation of shells, mines, other munitions and drones on a significant scale,” the Ukrainian president said.

Finland’s president said he did not believe Russia would risk an attack against a ⁠Nato country, with Alexander Stubb telling the Bild newspaper that it would “make no sense” to test the resolve of the alliance. “I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” ​he told Bild, adding that he ‌did not believe that Russia “would ever want to attack Nato, the world’s most powerful military ‌alliance”.

Stubb, whose country joined Nato in 2023, said the alliance had to be prepared for any scenario but he did not believe Moscow was in a position to go to war with Nato. “It makes no sense ​for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance.”

item.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina Toossi
item.description:
As with its approach to Hormuz, the US has mistaken applying pressure for an actual strategy. But Tehran has chips of its own to play

Donald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.

There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.

Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issues

item.title: UK to unveil 'comprehensive' response to Israeli West Bank settlement plans in coming weeks
item.description:
LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Britain will set out a "comprehensive" package of measures on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in the coming weeks, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Tuesday.

Miliband told lawmakers that Israel's E1 settlement project would cut across land which the Palestinians seek for a state and "risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

"This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution," he said. "We will act and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks."

item.title: Syria site infrastructure 'consistent with nuclear reactor': IAEA
item.description:
A Syrian site held infrastructure "consistent with a nuclear reactor", the UN nuclear watchdog said in a confidential report seen by AFP on Tuesday, adding that the country under ousted former leader Bashar al-Assad "failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities".

Inspectors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir Ezzor and a second location related to nuclear material identified by Syria.

item.description:

item.title: After over 200 days at sea, U.S. aircraft carrier arrives in Thailand
item.description:
LAEM CHABANG, Thailand, Sept 2 (Reuters) - U.S. Navy aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln steamed into Thailand'sLaem Chabang on Wednesday morning after more than 200 days at sea, including a long deployment in the Middle East, amid reports of mental health concerns and deteriorating conditions aboard.

The Lincoln, with roughly ​5,000 sailors and Marines aboard, has set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to ​Democratic lawmakers.

Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months, but during times of conflict that can be extended.

item.title: UN faces contentious Iran nuclear vote ahead of General Assembly
item.description:
By David Brunnstrom

Sept 1 (Reuters) - France said on Tuesday the U.N. Security Council will vote this month on renewing the mandate of a panel monitoring sanctions on Iran, setting up a potential showdown with Russia and China, which oppose the sanctions regime and oversight mechanisms.

The mandate of the panel, which supports the work of the U.N. sanctions committee on Iran, is due to expire on September 26, during the annual meeting of world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran is expected to top the agenda.
